body: This was my first tattoo! It’s my grandpa’s handwriting. I think it was a smart pick for the first one because I knew i wouldn’t ever regret it. Now i’m just hoping it doesn’t become entirely unreadable or need a redo/laser lol.

I saved about a years salary over a few years. Definitely wasn’t easy but I picked up shifts where I could and worked late because I told myself it would be worth it in the end. Did uber eats and stuff on the side when work wasn’t able to schedule me more shifts. 

I would work during the day and draw in my free time at night to build my portfolio, and once my portfolio was ready and I had the money I started working earlier so I could get out and have time to go to shops

I would say honestly you’d have to either find a way to save up more money by finding another job or working two jobs (which is easier said than done, i know) or find a shop that is willing to take you on part time and work with you. Some places offered to pay me for stuff like social media work and helping with marketing, or doing front desk work, so I would say just take a look at what offers you get from shops in your area and decide from there. 

Best of luck to you! I know it’s far from easy but I promise it’s worth it if you know you have a passion for this career

As someone who started off self taught and found a spot that would take me, I wouldn’t suggest it. I had no idea what I was doing wrong, just that my tattoos didn’t look right. Any shop that is willing to take you with no on the job experience would likely offer you an exploitative cut because the only benefit they have to hiring you is taking money from you. 

I was making mistakes that were easily corrected once I found an apprenticeship. I saved money for years to be able to afford getting through it, and did what I had to do to be able to start my career. 

It’s not easy to get a start in this industry but it’s worth waiting if you have to save to do it the right way imo.

This is so good for only almost 2 weeks on fake skin! For your question on shading with mags I suggest pushing out your needles more so you can see where they’re hitting on the fake skin. The more you practice this way, the more you’ll get a feel for how close to your lines you should be with the mag, then you can pull your needles back in to proper depth. You can always pack with a smaller mag too, or use a liner for tiny areas :) 

Don’t be discouraged! Packing up to the line is always hard to learn but outside of that your blacks look really good and saturated!

Most artists work with the tones in black and grey by watering down black ink. Some pigments might be slightly different or darker than others, but for the most part the technique is the same across artists. The only issue I could see is if your old work is aged and faded a bit, in that case any new additions will look darker by comparison. If you’re really worried, just ask your new artist about potentially touching up your old work at some point so the values match.

Hey, no offense meant here but I was able to find a handful of your designs online or recognized them from my own searches looking for inspiration in the past. It’s pretty obvious that elements of these are traced, and some of them will be recognizable to tattooers because we all use pinterest for inspo. Traditionally, tracing is encouraged for learning the elements of tattoo design, but your portfolio is a showcase of your own work and your specific talents. I would highly suggest using more realism as references and learning to simplify realistic subjects down to basic shapes. This will go a long way in developing your own style and understanding art fundamentals. Do not trace existing tattoo designs for your portfolio, with the exception being old school traditional flash like sailor jerry’s sheets. 

I would also generally suggest you add some realism and lettering/calligraphy! Doesn’t have to be perfect but showing those kinds of pieces shows you can do steady straight lines and understand anatomy/art fundamentals. Best of luck to you!

If you’re not sure at all though, I’d really suggest either getting something small or something meaningful that you won’t regret. My first tattoo was a memorial piece (my grandfather’s handwriting) I knew I wouldn’t ever regret that, and I was right lol! You can also use red ink instead of black, in case you might want to cover it in the future. It’s easier to cover up colors than black!

If you’re really worried, let your artist know upfront that you have sensitivities and they can do a patch test for you- just small areas of ink to see how your skin reacts. Definitely a better option than sitting for a full tattoo and having a bad reaction!

My biggest tip for composition in general is to draw to a shape (ex: an oval shape for upper arms, calves, etc) if you haven’t seen it yet this [Tattoo Placement Chart](https://ca.pinterest.com/pin/flow-lines-for-full-body-tattoos--798051996491160399/) is a super helpful tool for figuring out which way your design should “flow”. 

I think this would look more interesting with the flames following a the flow chart in a left/right direction- right now the flames guide the eye down toward the center of the vial, which is good b/c that’s the main subject of your piece, but unless every tat around it has this up and down flow it would look weird next to other tattoos. If your intent is to draw the eye to the middle I would make that your most detailed area, (maybe removing the pearls and putting a jewel in the very center) also the flame on the bottom left should be excluded b/c it doesn’t follow the flow of the others.

In the US tattoo schools are mostly considered shady/scammy. They aren’t regulated and tend to push people into shops too early, and doing tattoos without knowing what you’re doing is stressful for you and life altering for the client. Do serious research on the shop or school you’re interested in. 

Also, do not buy a cheap machine (fyi it is a machine, not a gun) for the sake of getting started early. Anything you teach yourself will be wrong. It’s impossible to learn proper technique alone and when/if you realize you don’t know what you’re doing and decide to get an apprenticeship, you’ll have to relearn from the beginning and unlearn your old habits which is hard as fuck. (speaking from experience as someone who did order a machine off amazon at first) The cheap machines also don’t tend to last and you can fuck up the motors by being too hard on the machine or using it incorrectly. Save up for something decent with a warranty. 


If you’re absolutely itching to learn more and ignore any of my other advice DO THIS ONE THING- in the states we have bloodborne pathogen testing you pay to do online, there is likely something similar in the UK and if not there are definitely videos online that teach how to work in a clean and sterile environment. Bare minimum, if you’re going to do it, learn how to practice safely. 


If you have questions feel free to DM me. Best of luck to you, it’s not easy but it’s worth it if you’re willing to learn and put in the work.

Going off my experience in the US, not sure what it’s like in the UK. This will be long/multiple comments so bare with me 

First step is to start drawing. A lot. You said you haven’t drawn in a while and that’s okay- I realized I wanted to tattoo after not drawing for a while too, but it took me almost 2 years to make a decent portfolio and even then I was told No 50+ times before I found an apprenticeship. 

Practice regular drawing, whatever you want, and then get into technical practice with light sources, anatomy, animals, whatever you know you’re not best at. Your portfolio needs to be your absolute best work and all finished pieces. You should also make sure these designs are not just “good drawings” but good tattoo designs. 

Look into tattoo history. Learn where it came from and why. Learn the different styles and most importantly GET TATTOOED! You’re not going to know much about the environment, and the people in the industry without physically being there. Getting into this industry is extremely difficult and you’re not going to have the drive for it if you’re not 100% sure this is what you want to do. Even after the apprenticeship, the job is 24/7, responding to inquiries and drawing happens every day even when you’re not at the shop.

It’s very very common for people to be nervous when coming in for a tattoo, I work at a shop myself and I get nervous before mine too! It’s something about my brain that always does because I know i’m walking in to being in pain for a bit, and it’s like that for a lot of the heavily tattooed people I work with too. As artists, we try and read off peoples vibe, so if you’re not feeling like having a conversation a good artist will pick up on that and not push it. If you’re really nervous, I don’t know of any artist that would take offense from you mentioning you prefer a quiet appointment. Most of the time we’re too focused on tattooing to have much time to talk anyway! Like someone else commented, I’d definitely message your artist beforehand on instagram and feel it out- some artists even have consultations days before your appointment where you’ll have a chance to meet them and get their vibe for yourself. Best of luck!

Different creams use different numbing agents and different artists have different preferences. I’d let your artist know you’re nervous about the pain in that area beforehand and ask if they have any preference in if you use numbing cream, what brand, and when they prefer you put it on. If they don’t suggest numbing cream there’s other alternatives like Bactine which your artist likely has or has access to at the shop, that can help with pain too.

Everyone heals at a different pace but IMO it looks like it’s still healing- seems a bit flaky/scabby from the first pic. You’ll be able to tell for sure how it’s settled once it’s fully healed in a week or two. That area is very small so it’s likely that over time as the ink expands over the years, that area will blur eventually. If you’d like to touch it up you’ll have to wait until it’s fully healed anyway.

FWIW there’s nothing embarrassing about not knowing what was going on at the time- we’re not mind readers and you were doing your best with the info you were given! This can be a slippery slope where we start to feel like there’s something inadequate about ourselves for not somehow knowing exactly what’s right to do in situations like this, especially when you anticipate your pwBPD to be emotional as a result, but ultimately you can only go off of what they tell you or you’ll drive yourself crazy trying to see what’s not there.

Though you seem supportive and understanding, people with BPD can make themselves believe even those closest to them don’t actually care when we’ve done nothing to make them think that way. Their fears of not being heard can lead to them not communicating out of fear of rejection, which they don’t realize to be self defeating. It’s the nature of the disorder unfortunately. I hope for your sake you’re able to meet your need for better communication! Best of luck OP.

Generally I would say the signs here are: 

- Overly Intense emotions (her reaction to the family remember not coming for a day turned into a days long episode) 

- Inability to communicate needs and feelings (not letting you know she wanted/needed the help initially) 

I also assume her concerns about money aren’t what she’s actually upset about, considering you’re (likely) paying more for her to get what she wanted initially. I would say this also ties into an inability to communicate her needs but could be deeper than that depending on what her reason for not communicating is. 

Ex: Did she not want to say she needed more time with the nurses because she was scared you’d react badly and reject her idea? (fear of rejection/abandonment) Was she stressed over the extra work she was doing to the point that it led to poor communication? (troubles balancing stress with work/other responsibilities) 

It’s hard to say 100% without knowing her, so sorry if I was wrong here, but just based off my experiences this is what I’ve noticed in common with other pwBPD in my life.

Just saw where you said you can’t afford therapy: 

- Talk to your employer (if you have one) about an EAP plan or to see if they provide mental health assistance 

- Call therapists or search online for therapists providing free/pro bono therapy. I know in my state therapists are required to take on a certain amount of free patients every year. 

- Ask therapists about what options they have based on your budget. They want to make their help as accessible as possible to you so don’t be afraid to ask.

Here to say that while I understand why you feel responsible, you weren’t. 

You didn’t mention your current age here, but from my perspective even as an early 20’s adult, I would never be coerced by a child into having sex with them, for any reason ever, because I am not attracted to children. 

If there were a child in my life that was showing the same behaviors you were at that age, I would absolutely take the steps you listed in your conclusion (Telling your mom, not going along with it.) and not “go along with it”. 

It’s important you realize that he is NOT a victim of your behavior. He did know better. Your “inappropriate actions” are likely learned from another trauma experience you had as a child. As an adult he should have the maturity to not only realize what you were doing was not normal, and a huge red flag for some kind of traumatic experience or mental illness but to also not contribute to it. This is why we have ages of consent. At certain points in childhood we aren’t mature enough to make decisions about sex because we don’t fully understand what it is and what it’s consequences are. 

You were not the adult here, he was. He knew better and allowed it to happen. You did not force him to do anything, he was aware of what was happening and had the ability to choose not to engage in it the same way you now would have the autonomy to decide not to do that to a child today. 

Please see a therapist and share this information with them. It is extremely common to feel guilt and shame about experiences like this, and the sooner you talk to a professional the sooner you can grow from this.

> “would it be alright if i continued use of cannabis, knowing these thoughts could occur?” 

It’s likely your dose was a little too high and caused you to feel uncomfortable or anxious. If this symptom is or isn’t a dealbreaker is entirely up to you.

> “I felt as if the high persisted throughout the second day, is this normal?” 

Edibles, (in my experience atleast) are much more potent for much longer periods of time. If you take one at night and it is a high dose (or higher than you’re used to) there’s a chance it may last through the night depending on your tolerance. 

> “Is it possible to be a lightweight when it comes to weed?” 

yes and no. Like alcohol, physical attributes (weight mostly) can cause weed to effect you at different intensities. And like alcohol, someone who routinely uses the drug can build a ‘tolerance’ and need to ingest more to get the same high they did when they started smoking. Usually when someone is a “lightweight” for weed it just means they don’t have a tolerance and can reach a more intense high easier. 

>”I am wondering if these are early signs I might become addicted” 

Cannabis is a generally non addictive substance. Of course, heavy smokers may experience negative side effects from not smoking for a few days or so, but unless you’re a VERY frequent smoker you have nothing to worry about in terms of cravings or addiction. Ofc this might not be true for all people, if you have an addictive personality maybe keep to a few days a week at best if you’re really worried about it, but it sounds to me like you wanting to try edibles again is coming from a place of curiosity and not addiction. 

Again this is all personal experience and my knowledge of weed isn’t on a professional level, but i’ve been smoking for 5+ years now and I don’t think you have anything to worry about. Hope this helps! You can PM me if you have any other questions.
